 Drought conditions spur early harvest for most Arkansas crops

 Harvesting cotton near England, Arkansas. Photo courtesy of Arkansas Farm Bureau.
 Hot and dry weather has caused drought like conditions throughout the state and it has aided harvest efforts. The state’s top crop at more than 3 million acres, soybeans, is virtually harvested along with corn and rice, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Crop Progress Report.
 The cotton crop is mostly harvested and it could be done by the end of next week. The dry weather has plunged down water levels along the Mississippi River and it might have an impact on grain movement along the river.
 “Fortunately for us, our harvest is about done,” said Scott Stiles, extension economics program associate for the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture. “Corn and rice have finished up. Soybeans are 87% done and cotton is 63% finished.”
 Soybeans were well ahead of the five-year average of 69%. Cotton’s five-year average is 53%, the report noted.
 “Cotton harvest progress took a near 20% jump from last week’s report,” said Zachary Treadway, extension cotton and peanut agronomist for UADA. “The dry weather has allowed pickers to roll from early in the mornings to late at night. It has been a very kind harvest season,” he said. “I expect another large jump in next week’s report. Reports are trending positive for both yield and quality from this year’s cotton crop. Barring some unforeseen hiccup, I foresee cotton harvest wrapping up before Halloween.”
 The weather also helped move peanuts to 34% harvested, but still behind the five-year average of 38%.
 “Peanut harvest is moving along briskly as well,” Treadway said. “Yields have been down some this year, as was to be expected after the summer we had.”
 The slower pace in harvest may have been due to uncertainty about whether a peanut processing facility in Jonesboro would continue to operate, Treadway said. Delta Peanut received a $5 million loan from the state to get through the 2026 season.
 “There would be no need to dig the crop just to disc it under,” Treadway said. “I think if we would have had certainty going into harvest, we would be further along. The uncertainty on processing has cleared up for the time being, which has allowed the crop a place to go, and I think that has helped kick harvest into high gear as well.”
 Dry weather is predicted to continue during the next week in the Arkansas Delta, according to the National Weather Service. Temperatures are projected to be in the upper 70s to low 80s during the next week with almost no chance of rain throughout the region.
 These drought conditions have led to lower levels on the Mississippi River.
 Over the past five years, low Mississippi River levels have impaired shipping and spiked shipping prices. UADA researchers have linked low Mississippi River levels to weakened basis for crops brought to elevators near the river.
 “The Mississippi River has not posed an issue for our growers this fall,” Stiles said. “However, a lengthy stretch of low river levels could hamper export movement of soybeans and other grains in the weeks ahead.”
 Stiles said that for the week ending Oct. 15, about 1.5 million metric tons of grain were exported from the Mississippi Gulf.
 “Sixty-five percent of the total was soybeans and nearly 60% of the soybeans were headed to China, which is welcome news for Arkansas growers,” he said. “For the 2026 marketing year, the U.S. has sold just over 414 million bushels of soybeans to China, compared to zero at this time last year.”
 The Mississippi River to the gulf also saw some wheat and corn exports last week.
 “Corn accounted for about 30% of export shipments last week,” Stiles said. “Most of it was headed to Colombia and Mexico. U.S. corn export sales are struggling and are currently 33% behind last year. However, the recent decline in corn prices is uncovering some fresh export demand as U.S. prices are becoming more competitive with Argentine values.”
 On Monday, the river was at 5 feet but was projected to drop to minus 4.2 feet by Nov. 4.
 The record low of minus 12 feet for the Mississippi River at Memphis was set in 2023.
 “The Mississippi River gauge at Memphis looks to fall into negative territory early next week,” Stiles said. “It’s something that bears watching during the peak U.S. grain export window.”
